newsitem.title: FRANCE: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE ACCUSES RIVALS OF INSINCERITY.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE ACCUSES RIVALS OF INSINCERITY.

text.p: Canadian Jacques Villeneuve sparked a new Formula One controversy on Friday, accusing his rival drivers of expressing insincere sadness after Oliver Panis's crash and saying that the sport had become too politically correct.

Villeneuve, who was reprimanded by the sports ruling body the International Automobile Federation (FIA) two weeks ago for his colourful and outspoken criticism of the 1998 rule changes, said he felt that Panis's injuries -- two broken legs -- were not something to cause serious concern.

"I'm disappointed at how politically correct Formula One has become," said Villeneuve, before finishing fifth behind world championship leader Michael Schumacher in rain-hit practice for Sunday's French Grand Prix.
"When someone has an accident, everyone acts as if they are sad -- but they don't really care."
Panis suffered double fractures to both of his legs when he crashed his Prost car during the Canadian Grand Prix. The Frenchman was now back with his family in Britanny.
"As a driver you know the risk is there every time you go out," Villeneuve said. "I am not saying it should be more dangerous but when you think about it two broken legs is not that bad.
"That happens to everyone at some point in their life."
Villeneuve's father Gilles was killed in practice for the Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder in 1982.

Schumacher, who said that Panis's accident in Canada had revived images of Ayrton Senna's death at Imola in 1994, denied he had not shown genuine feeling when he appeared saddened after winning in Montreal.
"I was genuinely concerned when I saw Olivier," the German said. "You are not human if that sort of incident does not affect you."

Villeneuve added he had not joined the 'drivers' union', the Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GPDA), because "I don't agree with what they are doing...I don't want to be part of something just because it exists."

The Canadian's words typified his independent streak as much as his hair-style. He had his brown hair bleached white in Monte Carlo earlier this week and cut an easily-recognisable figure in the pits and paddock.

Villeneuve, who drives a Williams, vowed earlier this month he would continue to speak his mind despite receiving a warning from FIA for ridiculing their plans for grooved tyres and narrower cars next season.
"I've not been asked to change my views or to stop expressing them," he said a day after the hearing in Paris. "But I have to change the way in which I put them in words.
He had said: "I know I can't say things any more like the regulations are stupid, or anything like that.
"I realise now I will have to take a deep breath, think more slowly and consider the words I am using."
